title: Night Shift Files After Dark: Assignment Fort Meade — Psychic Spies, Researching Paranormal Abilities and Stories of the Unexplained
byline: Declassified records document the military’s remote-viewing research at Fort Meade. In a separate strand of the story, people who lived and worked on the post have shared accounts of voices, figures and other unsettling experiences.
excerpt: FORT MEADE, Md. (First Alert Nation)- As Halloween activities bring people out after dark this weekend, Night Shift Files turns to a place with two very different kinds of eerie
content:
FORT MEADE, Md. (First Alert Nation)- As Halloween activities bring people out after dark this weekend, Night Shift Files turns to a place with two very different kinds of eerie stories: Fort George G. Meade.  Declassified government records document a real military mission to investigate psychic spying on the base. Factor in local stories of the unexplained from resident's tales of unexplained encounters, for the latest installment of The Night Shift Files. 

A little historical background to set the scene. Fort Meade is in western Anne Arundel County, near Odenton and between Baltimore and Washington. The installation opened as Camp Meade in 1917 to train soldiers for World War I. During World War II, German and Italian prisoners of war were held there; some died in captivity and were buried at the post. 

One of the base’s most unusual assignments is documented in declassified government files. During the Cold War, military and intelligence programs explored remote viewing—the claimed ability to describe distant or hidden places through extrasensory perception. The Army’s INSCOM program's work at Fort Meade ran under program names that included Grill Flame and Center Lane before later becoming part of the broader effort known as Stargate. Declassified records identify Fort Meade facilities used by the programs and describe remote-viewing sessions conducted for intelligence taskings.

The work moved beyond the laboratory to real world during moments of international crisis like during the 1979 Iran hostage crisis. Records say Fort Meade’s remote viewers conducted more than 200 sessions related to the effort to gather information about the hostages. A later review of the program found the results inconsistent and not reliable enough to support intelligence operations.

Despite the official government reports, former operators have come forward in recent years to tell their stories. They maintain that the programs were real missions that did solve cases and assist in cold war operations abroad. 

But the documented government research into the paranormal is only one part of Fort Meade’s strange history. The ghost stories we're about to share come from a different source: personal accounts shared online by people who say they lived or worked on the installation.

Military-life writer Army Wife 101 has dozens of recollections from former residents of Potomac Place. In one account, a parent described a young child waking before dawn and asking why a man had taken her mother’s lipstick into a closet. Another resident recalled hearing a voice from upstairs while searching for a child who was actually outside with his father. Other accounts describe footsteps heard through a baby monitor, a figure disappearing at the top of a staircase and a phone reportedly flying from a microwave and landing on the floor. These are residents’ recollections, not official reports, but they are now engrained forever as a part of Fort Meade’s ghost lore. (armywife101.com). 

One prominent figure in online Fort Meade lore is known as Elizabeth. Accounts describe her as a blonde woman in a peach-colored dress, reportedly seen near a building identified as the Child Development Services facility. The stories say she is still seen by visitors in the building that was once an Army barracks.

Other online tales refer to the former Oak Hill Youth Center, sometimes associated with the old Portland Hospital. People describe clanging sounds, ghostly appearances and objects seeming to move inside an abandoned section. The accounts vary, and the site is not an invitation to investigate.

The two strands of Fort Meade’s extensive paranormal history are distinct and there isn't enough room in one article to cover them all. One section belongs to the historical record of paranormal government research on the base; the other lives on in local lore of real paranormal activity from residents and workers.

Have you lived or worked at Fort Meade and experienced something you still can’t explain? Share your story with First Alert Nation for a future Night Shift Files installment.

We are not encouraging anyone to attempt to have an experience ! A warning before you go looking: Fort Meade is an active military installation and the home of National Security Agency headquarters. It is not a public ghost-hunting destination. Current Army guidance says visitors without a military or Department of Defense credential need a valid reason to enter, must provide valid identification and are subject to a background check. Entry is controlled, and visitors must follow the installation’s access procedures. 

Do not trespass, enter restricted areas or drive onto the installation to investigate a haunting. Unauthorized access could lead to arrest and criminal charges. If you are on post for approved business, obey all posted signs, speed limits and instructions from security personnel and military police—especially near NSA facilities. A quest to experience the unexplained is no reason to break the law or put yourself, officers or installation personnel at risk.
